442.title: Job, a good man (Job 1–2)
442.hook: a good man loses everything, and still does not curse God
442.carry: the lord gave, the lord took
442.howItsDone: Christians often read the book of Job in times of grief and suffering, and Job's words "the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away" are said at many Christian funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five books of the Psalms. Your line was every feeling has a psalm. Which one did you choose for this week? Today we leave the Psalms for the hardest book of wisdom. Day four hundred forty-two.

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." It opens like a folk tale, once upon a time, far away. Nobody knows for sure where Uz was. The book never says Job was an Israelite. He's just a man, somewhere east, with seven sons, three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, and a habit of getting up early to offer sacrifices in case his children had sinned at their parties. Then, in a single day, four messengers arrive, one on the heels of the next. Raiders took the oxen. Fire fell on the sheep. Raiders took the camels. And the last one: a great wind hit the house where his children were eating, and they are all dead.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.` → `FOUR MESSENGERS, ONE DAY.` → `EVERYTHING GONE.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible describes Job as "perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." Perfect here means whole, blameless, not flawless. Before the disasters, the reader is shown something Job never sees: a scene in heaven. The heavenly beings come before God, and among them is one called, in Hebrew, ha-satan. The satan, with the word the in front, more like a job title than a name: the adversary, the accuser. Christians have long identified him with the devil; many scholars read him here as a member of the heavenly court whose role is to accuse. God points out Job, and the accuser asks the question the whole book turns on: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Is anyone good for free, or only for the reward? Take it all away, and see. So it is taken. And Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground and worships: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Then his own body is struck with sores, and he sits in ashes scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery. His wife, who has also just buried ten children, says: curse God, and die. And Job answers: "shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" Here's what matters for the days ahead. The reader knows about the heavenly scene. Job never finds out. He has to live through all of it without the explanation.
screen: `PERFECT: WHOLE, BLAMELESS` · `HA-SATAN: THE ACCUSER` · `DOTH JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOUGHT?` · `JOB NEVER SEES THE REASON` · then, large: `THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone suffering undeservedly. Sit, and settle. Bring to mind someone whose trouble makes no sense. A child who is sick. A friend whose life fell apart through no fault of their own. People in the news who lost everything in a single day. Don't try to explain it. Job's story begins by refusing to. Just hold them steadily in mind. If you pray, you can name them before God and leave the why unanswered. If you don't, wish them strength, and let your attention rest on them, like a hand on a shoulder. The bell holds the time.
Job. A good man from the land of Uz who loses everything, and whose book asks whether anyone loves God for nothing.
Your line: the Lord gave, the Lord took. Today, notice one thing you hold that you didn't earn and can't keep forever, and handle it gently. Day four hundred forty-two.

options: curse God and walk away.
tear your robe, fall to the ground, and worship.

fork.reveal: Job grieves with his whole body and still blesses God's name. the demands for an answer come later, and the book keeps those too.

what it means: a good man loses everything, grieves, and still blesses God, without ever learning why.
what a scholar hears: ha-satan with the article, the accuser in the heavenly court, asking whether anyone fears God for nothing.

443.title: Seven days of silence (Job 2:11–13)
443.hook: his friends sit with him for a week without speaking; that's the best thing they do
443.howItsDone: Christians practice a ministry of presence by visiting the sick and the grieving, staying at wakes and sitting with the dying; many pastors and hospital chaplains point to Job's friends' silent week as the model.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job in the ashes, still blessing God's name. Your line was the Lord gave, the Lord took. What did you handle gently? Day four hundred forty-three.

You've been there, or you will be. The funeral home. The hospital corridor. The kitchen of a friend whose marriage just ended. You walk in with a casserole or a card, and your mind is racing for the right thing to say. Everything sounds wrong. They're in a better place. It'll get easier. Everything happens for a reason. You open your mouth, close it again. Most of us panic in that silence and fill it with something. Three men in the book of Job, at least at first, did something braver. They said nothing at all. For a week.
screen: `THE HOSPITAL CORRIDOR.` → `RACING FOR THE RIGHT WORDS.` → `THREE MEN SAY NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible: "Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him." Notice that. They made an appointment. They coordinated, traveled from three different places, and arrived together, on purpose. Then they see him from a distance, and they don't recognize him. Disease and grief have changed him that much. So they weep aloud, tear their robes, and throw dust into the air over their heads, the signs of mourning. And then this: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." On the ground, in the ash, at his level. Seven days was the length of deep mourning in the Bible; Joseph mourned his father Jacob for seven days. Jews still keep that week of sitting with mourners today, called shiva, from the Hebrew for seven. Here's the detail many readers love. The friends don't speak until Job speaks first. They follow his lead. And here's the sad part, which the next days will show: once they open their mouths, it goes badly. Many readers have said that the week of silence was the best comfort they gave. Paul's letter to the Romans puts the same instinct simply: "weep with them that weep."
screen: `THEY MADE AN APPOINTMENT` · `THEY DIDN'T RECOGNIZE HIM` · `ON THE GROUND, SEVEN DAYS` · `NOT ONE WORD` · then, large: `FOR THEY SAW THAT HIS GRIEF WAS VERY GREAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with someone without fixing. If someone near you is hurting and you can be with them today, go, and let silence be allowed. For now, in this sit, picture them. Imagine sitting down beside them, on the floor if that's where they are. Notice the urge to say something helpful. Let it rise and fall without acting on it. Just be there, breathing near them. If you pray, you can hold them before God without words. If you don't, simply keep them company in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Seven days of silence. Job's three friends sit on the ground with him for a week, and not one of them speaks.
Your line: they sat with him. Today, when someone tells you something painful, resist the first helpful sentence. Stay quiet a moment longer, and let them lead. Day four hundred forty-three.

444.title: Let the day perish (Job 3)
444.hook: Job curses the day he was born, and the Bible keeps his words
444.howItsDone: Many Christians pray laments, honest complaints brought to God, using the words of Job, the psalms of lament and Lamentations, and some churches hold services of lament after tragedies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three friends on the ground with Job for seven days, saying nothing. Your line was they sat with him. Did you let someone lead, and stay quiet a moment longer? Day four hundred forty-four.

People say it when someone puts up with a lot: she has the patience of Job. The phrase comes from the letter of James in the New Testament, and it paints a picture of a man who suffers quietly, never raising his voice. Hold on to that picture for a moment. Because after seven days of silence on the ground, Job finally speaks. And the first thing out of his mouth, the opening of the long poem at the heart of the book, is not patient. It is not quiet. It is one of the darkest speeches anywhere in the Bible.
screen: `THE PATIENCE OF JOB.` → `SEVEN DAYS OF SILENCE END.` → `NOT WHAT ANYONE EXPECTS.`

segments.voice: Chapter three begins, in the King James Bible: "After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day." Not God. His day. The day he was born. "Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived." He wants that day erased from the calendar, the stars of that night to stay dark, the dawn never to come. Then the questions: "Why died I not from the womb?" Why is light given to someone in misery? And near the end, the line many sufferers have recognized: "For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me." Here's the striking thing about the book's shape. Chapters one and two are prose, like a story. Right here, with this curse, the book switches to poetry, and it stays poetry for almost forty chapters. The pain gets the poetry. And the Bible keeps every word. It doesn't cut this chapter or soften it. The prophet Jeremiah says something close, in his own book: cursed be the day wherein I was born. Two people of faith, saying the unsayable, and scripture keeps both. Now back to James. The Greek word translated patience there is hupomone. It means endurance, staying under a weight without walking away. That fits Job better than quiet ever did. Job never stops talking to God, even when he's shouting. He doesn't leave. Christians have often called this kind of speech lament, prayer that tells God the truth about how bad it is. On this reading, even a curse on your birthday, said to God, is still a way of staying in the conversation.
screen: `HE CURSES HIS DAY, NOT GOD` · `FROM PROSE INTO POETRY` · `THE BIBLE KEEPS EVERY WORD` · `PATIENCE MEANS ENDURANCE` · then, large: `LET THE DAY PERISH WHEREIN I WAS BORN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write your honest lament. Take a piece of paper, or your phone's notes. Write what is actually hard right now, in plain words. Don't tidy it. Don't add a lesson at the end. If you're angry, write angry. If you're tired of something, say so. A few lines is plenty. Then stop, and sit with what you wrote for the rest of the time. If you pray, you can offer it to God as it is, unpolished, the way Job did. If you don't, let it simply be true on the page. The bell holds the time.
Let the day perish. Job's first words after the silence: a curse on his birthday, kept whole in the Bible.
Your line: even this is prayer. Today, if something hard comes up, don't hide it from God or from yourself. Say it honestly, once, and let that count. Day four hundred forty-four.

445.title: Bad comfort (Job 4–5)
445.hook: his friends insist he must have sinned; they're wrong
445.tomorrow: I know that my redeemer lives
445.howItsDone: Christian pastors and chaplains often study Job's friends as a warning in pastoral care training: listen first, and do not tell sufferers their pain is a punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job cursing the day he was born, and the Bible keeping every word. Your line was even this is prayer. Did you say one hard thing honestly? Day four hundred forty-five.

Everything happens for a reason. God doesn't give you more than you can handle. Maybe this is a wake-up call. At least you're young. Most of us have heard sentences like these at the worst moment of our lives, or, if we're honest, said them. They're usually meant kindly. They come from people who love us and can't stand the silence. And they can land like a slap. The book of Job has a name for the people who say them, coined by Job himself. But first, the man who speaks right after Job's curse. His name is Eliphaz, and he's the gentlest of the three.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON.` → `MEANT KINDLY.` → `LANDS LIKE A SLAP.`

segments.voice: Eliphaz begins politely, almost apologetically: if we try to talk with you, will you be upset? Then he reminds Job that Job has comforted others in his time. Fair enough. Then the turn, in the King James Bible: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?" Think about it, Job. Innocent people don't get destroyed. "Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same." You reap what you sow. Do the math. He even describes a frightening night vision to back himself up: "Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up." And he has lines that sound like they belong on a wall: "Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward." Here's the strange part. A lot of what Eliphaz says is true somewhere. The apostle Paul even quotes him, in First Corinthians, as scripture. The problem isn't the sayings. It's where he points them. He takes a general rule and fits it onto a grieving man the reader knows is blameless. He explains Job's pain to Job. Job's reply comes a few chapters later: "miserable comforters are ye all." Centuries later, in John's Gospel, the disciples see a man born blind and ask Jesus: who sinned, this man, or his parents? Jesus answers: neither. And at the very end of the book of Job, God himself will say these friends got it wrong. They came to comfort. They sat in silence beautifully. Then they started explaining.
screen: `POLITE, ALMOST APOLOGETIC` · `WHO EVER PERISHED, BEING INNOCENT?` · `TRUE SAYINGS, WRONG MAN` · `MISERABLE COMFORTERS` · then, large: `THEY CAME TO COMFORT, THEN EXPLAINED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch yourself explaining someone's pain. Sit, and think back over the last few weeks. Was there a moment someone told you something hard, and you reached for a reason? Everything happens for a reason. Maybe it's for the best. At least. Find it, gently, without beating yourself up. Then replay the moment, and imagine saying instead: that sounds really hard. I'm here. Feel how different that is. If you pray, you can ask for the grace to sit before you speak. If you don't, just rehearse the quieter answer. The bell holds the time.
Bad comfort. Job's friends, meaning well, turn true-sounding sayings on a suffering man and tell him he must have deserved it.
Your line: don't explain their pain. Today, when someone shares something hard, catch the at least or the for a reason before it leaves your mouth, and just listen. Day four hundred forty-five.

screen: `DAY 445 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I KNOW THAT MY REDEEMER LIVES.`

446.title: I know that my redeemer lives (Job 19:25–27)
446.hook: in the depths, Job reaches for hope anyway
446.howItsDone: Christians often read Job 19:25 at funerals as a confession of hope in the resurrection, and many hear it sung each year in the soprano aria "I know that my Redeemer liveth" from Handel's Messiah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eliphaz and the comfort that hurt. Your line was don't explain their pain. Did you catch an at least before it left your mouth? Day four hundred forty-six.

By chapter nineteen, it's bad. The friends have stopped being gentle. Job says his brothers keep their distance, his servants ignore him, his breath is strange to his own wife, and little children mock him when he stands up. "Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me." Nobody does. And then he wishes for something odd. He wishes his words could be written down. Not just written: carved with an iron pen into rock, filled in with lead, so they'd last forever, so someone someday would know what he said. Here's the thing. His wish came true. What he says next has been read, sung and carved on gravestones for centuries.
screen: `FRIENDS GONE, FAMILY DISTANT.` → `CARVE MY WORDS IN ROCK.` → `THE WISH CAME TRUE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth." The Hebrew word for redeemer is go'el. It isn't a church word first. It's a family word. In Israel, a go'el was your nearest relative with a duty to you. If you fell into debt and had to sell your land, your go'el bought it back. If you were sold into slavery, your go'el paid to free you. If you were killed, your go'el made sure your blood didn't go unanswered. In the book of Ruth, Boaz is the go'el who buys back a family's land and marries the widow Ruth. So when Job, abandoned by family and friends, says my go'el lives, he's saying: somebody is still on my side. Someone will stand up for me at the end, even if nobody here will. Who is it? Readers have heard it differently. Christians, for many centuries, have heard Christ in this verse: the redeemer who lives and stands on the earth at the last day. Handel set it as the aria that opens part three of Messiah, and it is read at many Christian funerals. Jewish readers usually hear God himself as Job's defender. Some scholars think Job meant a heavenly witness, the advocate he mentions a few chapters earlier. And the next verse is one of the hardest in the Hebrew Bible to translate; it can be read as in my flesh shall I see God, or without my flesh. The King James Bible chose "yet in my flesh shall I see God." However it's read, a man at the bottom reaches up anyway.
screen: `GO'EL: THE FAMILY REDEEMER` · `BUYS BACK LAND, FREES THE SLAVE` · `CHRIST, GOD, OR A HEAVENLY WITNESS` · `A HOPE CARVED IN ROCK` · then, large: `I KNOW THAT MY REDEEMER LIVETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold on to one hope. Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you're hoping for that you can't make happen yourself. Healing. A reconciliation. Someone coming home. Justice for something that went wrong. Name it to yourself plainly. Now hold it the way Job holds his: not because the evidence is good, but because you refuse to let go. If you pray, you can say his line slowly: I know that my redeemer liveth. If you don't, simply keep the hope in your hands for the whole sit, like something carved. The bell holds the time.
Redeemer. In Hebrew, go'el: the family member who buys back what was lost and stands up for you when no one else will.
Your line: my redeemer lives. Today, be someone's go'el in a small way. Stand up for one person who has nobody speaking for them. Day four hundred forty-six.

447.title: Where is wisdom? (Job 28)
447.hook: men mine for silver and gold, but wisdom isn't found in the earth
447.carry: the fear of the lord is wisdom
447.howItsDone: Many Christians pray for wisdom before decisions and study, and Job 28 is read in some churches at services for teachers, students and the start of a school year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job carving a hope in rock. Your word was redeemer, and your line, my redeemer lives. Who did you stand up for? Day four hundred forty-seven.

Deep in the desert south of the Dead Sea, there are ancient copper mines, shafts cut straight down into rock thousands of years ago. Miners worked there by lamplight, far from any town, digging after a thin green vein. The book of Job knows that kind of work. In chapter twenty-eight, the arguing suddenly stops, and a poem begins about miners. They push back the darkness, it says. They cut shafts in places no traveler goes. They hang on ropes, swinging, far from other people. They turn mountains upside down by the roots and find sapphires in the dust. No hawk has seen these paths. No lion has walked them. Humans, the poem says, can reach almost anything. Almost.
screen: `SHAFTS CUT INTO ROCK.` → `MINERS ON ROPES.` → `HUMANS CAN REACH ALMOST ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: The poem opens, in the King James Bible: "Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it." Silver has a place. Gold has a place. Then the question that names today: "But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?" You can dig for it, but "The depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me." You can't buy it either. The poem piles up the treasures of the ancient world, gold, onyx, sapphire, coral, pearls, topaz, and sets them all aside: "the price of wisdom is above rubies." Even death and destruction say they've only heard rumors of it. So where is it? "God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof." Then the last verse, in which God speaks to humankind: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding." Fear here doesn't mean terror. The Hebrew is yirah: awe, reverence, the feeling of standing in front of something far greater than you. Notice what the poem is doing in the middle of Job's story. Job and his friends have spent twenty chapters trying to work out exactly why he's suffering, each sure he has the answer. This poem quietly says: nobody can dig that out. Real wisdom isn't a fact you extract. It starts with awe, and with turning away from harm. Scholars debate who speaks the poem, Job or the book's narrator; it reads like a pause, a breath in the argument. And it sounds the theme that the wisdom books, Proverbs especially, come back to again and again.
screen: `A VEIN FOR THE SILVER` · `THE DEPTH SAITH, IT IS NOT IN ME` · `ABOVE RUBIES` · `GOD KNOWETH THE PLACE` · then, large: `THE FEAR OF THE LORD, THAT IS WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for wisdom in one conversation. Before the sit, choose a conversation you'll have today, at work, at home, on the phone. During the sit, picture it. Who's there? Where do you usually rush, or argue, or try to win? Now picture going in with a little awe instead: listening for what you don't already know. Let your breathing slow. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom, in your own words or with the poem's last line. If you don't, set the simple intention to listen like a miner looks for a vein. The bell holds the time.
Where is wisdom? Job chapter twenty-eight's question: humans can mine almost anything, but wisdom begins in awe of God.
Your line: the fear of the Lord is wisdom. Today, in one conversation, listen for the thing you don't know yet, before you say the thing you do. Day four hundred forty-seven.

what it means: humans can mine almost anything, but wisdom starts with awe of God and turning from harm.
what a scholar hears: an interlude poem whose speaker is debated, ending in yirat Adonai, the motto the wisdom books return to.

448.title: The whirlwind (Job 38–39)
448.hook: God answers with questions: where were you when I laid the earth's foundations?
448.howItsDone: Christians often read God's speeches from the whirlwind in times of suffering and at services celebrating creation, and many find in them a call to humility and wonder rather than an explanation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, miners in the dark and wisdom no treasure can buy. Your line was the fear of the Lord is wisdom. In which conversation did you listen first? Day four hundred forty-eight.
screen: `THE FEAR OF THE LORD IS WISDOM.`

segments.voice: For thirty-five chapters, people have talked about God. The friends explained him. Job accused him, pleaded with him, demanded a hearing. Near the end of his last speech, Job all but signs his name to a legal complaint: oh that one would hear me, let the Almighty answer me. Then a young man named Elihu bursts in and talks for six chapters more. And then the sky changes. The wind picks up. Dust lifts off the ground and spins. And for the first time since the opening scenes in heaven, God speaks. Not to the friends. To Job. Out of a storm.
screen: `THIRTY-FIVE CHAPTERS OF TALK.` → `LET THE ALMIGHTY ANSWER ME.` → `THE SKY CHANGES.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said, Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?" And then God doesn't answer Job's questions. He asks his own. "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Who set its measurements? Who laid its cornerstone, "When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?" Who shut the sea behind doors and told it, "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed"? Have you walked the springs of the deep, seen the storehouses of the snow? "Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?" Then chapter thirty-nine turns to animals, and they're wild ones: lions hunting, mountain goats giving birth where no one sees, the wild donkey laughing at the city, the ostrich that leaves her eggs in the sand and still outruns the horse, the war horse itself: "hast thou clothed his neck with thunder?" Here's what's strange. God never mentions the scene in heaven, never explains the test. Job never finds out why. Instead, he's taken on a tour of a universe that is huge, wild and mostly not about humans at all. Readers hear this differently. Some hear a rebuke: who are you to question me? Some hear a kind of wonder, God sharing his delight in creation with a man who's only been staring at his own ashes. Some find it unsatisfying, and the book lets them. But one thing is plain. Job asked for God to answer. God came.
screen: `ANSWERED OUT OF THE WHIRLWIND` · `WHEN THE MORNING STARS SANG` · `PLEIADES, ORION, THE WILD GOAT` · `NO EXPLANATION, BUT GOD CAME` · then, large: `WHERE WAST THOU WHEN I LAID THE FOUNDATIONS OF THE EARTH?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something wild and huge. Step outside if you can and look up: the sky, clouds stacked high, a big old tree, the sea, the stars if it's dark. If you're stuck indoors, look out the farthest window, or call up a picture of a mountain or a galaxy. Let it be bigger than you. Let your problems sit in proportion for a minute, not erased, just smaller against the sky. Breathe. If you pray, you can let the question rest in you: where were you? If you don't, just let wonder have the time. The bell holds the time.
The whirlwind. The storm God speaks from at the end of Job, answering with questions about the stars, the sea and the wild animals.

Your line: where were you? This week walked with Job: a good man, seven days of silence, let the day perish, bad comfort, my redeemer, where is wisdom, and the whirlwind. Today, look up at the sky once and let it be bigger than your worry. Day four hundred forty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: God puts Job in his place.
what it means: God comes, as Job asked, and answers with questions and a tour of a wild creation, but never explains.
what a scholar hears: the speeches never mention the heavenly wager; readers hear rebuke, wonder or an unanswered question, and the book lets all stand.
